A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TERC research, despite a changed title and substantial reorganization. Their text, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support matching retained, added, and removed content.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic-data experiments, Secret Key Game and Gym evaluations, and Iterated Prisoner’s Dilemma experiments, including supplementary learning-dynamics results in Appendix H.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds CPU inference-speed measurements in Tables 1–2 and an empirical investigation of Condition 1 in Appendix B.

M1.justification: V2 removes the general subset-search procedure presented as Algorithm 1 in v1 Section 5.4, substantially narrowing the proposed algorithmic scope. V1’s practical sequential-selection Algorithm 2 becomes v2’s Algorithm 1 with the same operations; the TERC criterion, neural estimator, and null-model thresholding are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use the two synthetic redundancy datasets, Secret Key Game with 25 or 50 keys, three noise-augmented Gym environments, and TFNT opponents in the Iterated Prisoner’s Dilemma. The new timing and assumption analyses use retained environments rather than extending dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: UMFI with optimal transport and Permutation Importance remain the evaluated feature-selection comparators in the corresponding experiments. Full-state controls are also retained. SEEK and AMIFS-related work receive new discussion but are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: V2 adds distinct evaluation protocols: CPU inference benchmarking at batch sizes 1 and 64 with 10,000 calls, and a Condition 1 investigation using 10,000 state-action pairs, KSG or empirical mutual-information estimates, and unequal-sized subset comparisons. These extend evaluation beyond the retained feature-selection and learning-performance protocols; existing Appendix I training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V1 asserts that Condition 1 holds in its experiments without a dedicated empirical check. V2 Appendix B and Figure 11 add a cross-environment analysis intended to substantiate this assumption underlying the minimality guarantee. The existing training-stage interpretability and history-length analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both retain 10 measure-estimation runs, five RL runs, 95% confidence intervals, and the same normality-based null-model test in Appendix I.7. The new timing tables use five-seed averages, without introducing a different uncertainty-estimation procedure or reporting increased repetitions for existing experiments.

E6.justification: The original result plots and baseline findings are retained, but v2 adds a new family of deployment-efficiency results. Table 1 reports SKG-50 speedups of 2.60× and 2.20× at batch sizes 1 and 64; Table 2 reports Gym speedups spanning 1.03×–1.33×. Figure 11 additionally reports no detected Condition 1 violations under its proposed test.

T1.justification: V1’s assumption-free minimality theorem and its Appendix F proof are removed, while its practical conditional theorem becomes v2 Theorem 2. V2 also removes the separate transfer-entropy derivation and introduces Appendix B’s redundancy statistic and proposed Condition 1 test. These alter theoretical scope beyond notation and renumbering.

C1.justification: V2 drops the contribution claiming an assumption-free minimal-subset construction and emphasizes minimality under Condition 1. Its abstract and conclusion explicitly frame selection as policy-dependent and foreground retraining and inference efficiency, including the new 2.6× inference claim, instead of v1’s broader sample-efficiency framing.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly explains that selected variables depend on the learned policy and training algorithm, and that reported efficiency gains exclude initial full-state training. It also states that failure of Condition 1 sacrifices minimality while preserving information. These add useful applicability qualifications; the original interpretations of learning-stage behavior remain largely unchanged.

D1.justification: V1 promises a code release upon acceptance, whereas v2 supplies a concrete repository link. V2 additionally documents timing batch sizes and call counts and the sampling and estimation choices for Appendix B. Existing network architectures, hyperparameters, training budgets, and null-model implementation details are retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds focused positioning against AMIFS-based RL variable selection, SEEK, and recurrent approaches to partially observable state representation. It acknowledges exceptions to the earlier broad criticism of dimensionality-reduction methods, while removing portions of the abstraction literature discussion and the extended Catav/Janssen critique. The overall research positioning remains information-theoretic feature selection for RL.

P1.justification: V2 substantially condenses and reorganizes the narrative: it changes the title, compresses the background, separates CPMCR into its own section, introduces an explicit training/data-collection pipeline, and rewrites several experimental explanations. A terminology glossary and notation summary are also added.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a different journal layout with changed typography, headers, text width, and figure placement; Figures 3 and 4 now share a page. It adds two timing tables, a notation table, and the multi-panel Condition 1 figure. Original figures are retained, with appendix figures renumbered rather than replaced.

improvement.justification: V2 improves clarity about policy dependence and initial-training costs, adds deployment measurements, and supplies a code link. However, Appendix B claims to verify Condition 1 using an unconditional redundancy threshold R=H(A), without establishing equivalence to Equation 6’s conditional-entropy and irreducibility requirements; Figure 11 also introduces a sign inconsistency. The benefits coexist with an unresolved support gap in the new validation of a central guarantee, preventing a reliable net quality judgment.
